records.one_line: A claim counts only when it comes with the inputs it was computed from, a certificate showing how, and a checker that recomputes the result and accepts it; a claim stated with none of these counts for nothing.
records.deep: A result can be used as evidence only if someone can reconstruct it. The claim has to arrive with the inputs it was computed from and a certificate, and a separate checker has to recompute the verdict from them and accept it. The claim may then say no more than that check established. A confident sentence, a label copied from a test file or a model's own answer has the lowest possible standing until something independent works it out again.

formal.reads: A claim over a basis is admissible only if some certificate and checker accept it, with the claim's strength capped by the strength of that check; a claim that arrives with no certificate sits at the bottom of the evidence order. The condition is necessary, not sufficient: passing a check is what admission requires, never a promise that the claim is true.

records.one_line: A small checker that reads certificates decides whether a claim is trusted; the program that produced the certificate has no say in that decision.
records.deep: Trust sits in one small checker. A producer, however large or capable, emits a certificate, and a small, separately maintained checker reads it and decides. Because the deciding part stays small, the code that has to be audited stays small even as the producers grow, and a clever or broken producer cannot widen what gets accepted. A claim is as strong as what the checker examined, whatever the reputation of the program that generated it.

formal.reads: A claim is trusted only when some certificate is accepted by the designated checker, the checker is not the thing that produced the certificate, and the checker is small enough to audit and rerun.

records.one_line: Permission to cause an effect is worked out when the action happens, from the tokens presented, the policy, proof references and the current state; holding a long-lived credential gives no permission by itself.
records.deep: Permission is calculated at the moment of acting. For each requested effect, the authorizer looks up the tokens actually presented, the policy, the proof references and the current state of the system, and decides whether this effect is allowed. Identity, a long-lived key or a reachable tool count for nothing on their own. This matters most where a component holds broad power and is steered into using it for someone else, the confused-deputy problem, so the limit on each effect comes from its declared scope and approval.

formal.reads: Authority for a subject to cause an effect is the output of the authorizer's derivation over the dereferenced tokens, governing policy, proof references, and current world-state; a standing credential whose tokens dereference to nothing grants nothing. Possession is one input to the derivation, never the derivation.

records.refuses: Treating a long-lived credential as permission.

records.does_not_prove: These two authorizers cover their own kinds of effect; other effects in the system need their own authorization.

reader_ladder.potential_misread: That a valid credential is enough, when it is only one of the inputs used to decide this particular action.

records.one_line: A computed result is identified by a hash of the exact inputs it was computed from; matching inputs allow reuse, changed inputs force a recompute, and missing inputs mean no result.
records.deep: A cached or reused result is identified by a hash of the inputs it was computed from, so two results are the same only when those inputs are the same. A shared name or file path counts for nothing. When the hashes match, the stored result may be reused; when the inputs have changed, it is recomputed or rejected; when the inputs cannot be found, there is no result. Reusing an output because its name matches, after its inputs have changed, is how a stale summary or a tampered cache passes for fresh.

records.one_line: Something built from parts is trusted only as far as its weakest part, a part with no evidence counts as blocked, and a later stage may lower a status but can raise it only with new evidence.
records.deep: The status of a combined result is the lowest status among its parts, so one blocked or unchecked part holds the whole result down however many other parts pass. A part with no evidence counts as blocked. A later stage may lower a status at any time, but raising it needs a new check under AX-1. This is why the release step stops when it finds private material or overclaiming wording, and why an unchecked requirement is reported as blocked.

records.one_line: Failing to show that a claim is true does not show that it is false; an absence counts as a negative only inside a declared finite domain that has been checked completely.
records.deep: When a claim has not been shown, its status is unknown, which differs from refuted. An absence counts as a negative only when the domain was declared finite in advance and every item in it was checked, so that "nothing found" means "everything was looked at". Outside such a domain, a missing relation, an unmapped area or a fact with no cited source is recorded as an open gap that can be filled in later.

records.one_line: A calculation that is defined only under certain conditions returns a value when those conditions hold, and otherwise returns a labelled refusal with a reason and evidence, never an unexplained number or NaN.
records.deep: Numerical code often produces a plausible value when the conditions it needs do not hold. Here such a calculation must return one of two things. It returns a value when its declared precondition is met, and otherwise a refusal that names the reason and carries the evidence. A NaN, an out-of-range forecast horizon or a missing library then reaches the caller as a labelled refusal it can handle, instead of a figure that the next step prints as a result.

formal.reads: For every input: when the declared precondition holds, the computation returns Ok carrying some value; when it does not hold, the computation returns a typed Refusal carrying a reason and the evidence behind it. Both branches are total; there is no third, silent outcome.

records.one_line: A record of where a value came from, and how far it may be trusted, travels with the value across every step; untrusted material reaches a sensitive output only through a declared cleaning step.
records.deep: How far a value can be trusted depends on where it came from and what was done to it on the way. Each value carries a label giving its origin and the strongest claim it supports, and the label is passed along at every step. Untrusted material, such as a prompt, a reply from an outside provider or text from private files, can reach a public or privileged output only through a declared cleaning step whose result the output's policy accepts. A label added at the last step carries no weight unless it was carried all the way.

formal.reads: A derived value carries at least the restriction of what it was derived from; and for any flow into a sink, either the value's label already sits within the sink's policy, or the flow passes through a declared transform whose output label the sink's policy admits. The endpoint never stamps the label; the label arrives with the value.

records.one_line: A change counts as complete only if it has a way to be undone or is declared permanent; a change in several steps completes only while each step's expected starting state still holds and no one else is writing the same path.
records.deep: A write is accepted only once there is a way back from it, or an explicit statement that there is none. A change counts as complete if it comes with an undo step or is declared permanent. A change made in several steps is a saga: before each step, the step checks that the state it started from is still current (compare-and-swap) and that it is the only writer on that path. This stops a sequence that succeeds partway, then meets a newer state or a second writer, from leaving the system in a condition nobody chose and nobody can undo.

formal.reads: An effect may count as landed only if it declares a compensator or an irreversible boundary; and a multi-step effect lands only while the parent it expected still matches the head and at most one writer holds its path. Reversibility is not promised; what is required is that every effect declares which kind it is.

records.one_line: A statement about something that keeps changing is a stored reading, valid only while it records when it was taken, what it was read from, and how to read it again.
records.deep: A number describing a running system goes out of date as soon as the system changes, so every such number is treated as a stored reading. It must carry four things: the value, the time it was taken, the source it was read from and the rule for reading it again. Once the source no longer matches, the reading must be refreshed or withdrawn. Running counts and dashboard totals need this most, because readers assume they are current.

records.refuses: A count from a changing system stated with no date and no way to refresh it.

example.text: The fact-claim audit flags any changing number that carries no date or refresh rule with a fixed error code, so a live count cannot be published as current without saying when it was taken and how to recompute it.

counterexample.text: A page prints a running total once and leaves it up for weeks with no date and no way to recompute it, so an old reading looks like a live figure.

records.does_not_prove: Flagging undated numbers does not make any dated number current or correct, and the rule for refreshing this axiom's own figures has not been written yet.

reader_ladder.plain: A number about something that keeps changing is a reading taken at one moment. To be usable later it has to say when it was read, where it was read from and how to read it again.

analogy.text: An electricity meter reading is useful on a bill only if it records the date, which meter it came from and how to take a fresh reading. The bare number says nothing about today's usage.

records.one_line: A rule document may govern only when a program accepts its format and it lists the evidence it must produce and what it does not cover; a rule written only in prose is for reading.
records.deep: A standard, contract or rule has force only when a program that parses its grammar accepts its format, and when it lists the evidence it must produce and a statement of what it does not establish. A clause that is only well written has no force. The parser decides on the document's checkable structure, so the documents that define how claims are judged are held to the same discipline as the claims. Passing the parser shows only that the document is well formed, and reading a pass as complete coverage is itself rejected.

formal.reads: A doctrine artifact carries authority only when an executable grammar accepts its shape and it presents its evidence obligations and its own anti-claim; an artifact failing any of these sits in the projection tier, which can be read but cannot govern.

counterexample.text: A persuasive standard written in prose is treated as binding because it sounds authoritative, though no parser accepted its structure and it lists no evidence requirements or limits.

records.does_not_prove: A document that passes the parser is well formed; whether its content is complete or correct is a separate question.

reader_ladder.plain: A rule can govern only when it passes a fixed format check and lists the evidence it must produce and what it leaves out. A well-written paragraph on its own is something to read.

analogy.text: A customs declaration clears goods only when it passes the form check, comes with its supporting paperwork and states what it does not vouch for. A convincing letter describing the shipment clears nothing.

records.one_line: Every claim the system makes about itself must pass the same checks it applies to any other claim; its own reports and tools get no exemption.
records.deep: Every claim the system makes about itself, in a generated page, a validator, a saved result or a coverage report, must pass the same tests as any outside claim. The program that computes support is itself held to the support rules, and a page like this one, generated from the source, cannot give the source more authority than it has. Without an exemption, the system can state its own limits and that statement is checked like any other.

records.requires: That the system's own pages, validators, records and generated reports meet the same evidence and refusal rules as everything else.
records.refuses: An exemption for the system's own documents and tools.

example.text: The release wording gate applies the same wording rules to the system's own public text as to any other text, and blocks overclaiming wording in the system's own pages.

counterexample.text: A system publishes a self-assessment saying "verified and complete" that would fail the evidence rules it applies to the work it audits.

records.does_not_prove: Holding its own documents to the same rules removes the exemption; the system's limits remain, now written down.

reader_ladder.plain: The system holds its own statements about itself to the same standard it holds everyone else's. Being the one doing the checking earns it no discount.

analogy.text: A referee cannot switch to an easier rulebook when the call involves their own team. The same rules apply.

reader_ladder.potential_misread: That applying the rules to itself makes the system trustworthy, when it only removes the exemption.

records.one_line: Recompute a verdict from the evidence it was based on instead of repeating its label, and keep a deliberately false test case that the check has to reject.
records.deep: P-1 applies AX-1 to everyday building work. A fixture's own verdict, a route status, a count or a sentence of public copy is treated as a claim to recompute from the evidence underneath it. The false test case matters as much as the recomputation, because a check that has only ever seen passing input has never had the chance to reject anything. When this rule holds, a green status on the map means the verdict was recomputed.

formal.reads: Trust a verdict only when a checker recomputes it from the underlying evidence and that same checker rejects the negative fixture built to slip the cheap lie through.

records.governs: Whether a stated result may be used as evidence.
records.requires: Recomputing the verdict from lower-level evidence, and a negative test case that the checker rejects.
records.refuses: Repeating a declared verdict, label or count as if it had been checked.

example.text: The benchmark-integrity replay recomputes a score from the recorded run instead of trusting the reported number, and keeps known gaming attempts as test cases that the replay must catch.

counterexample.text: A summary copies a component's self-reported "passed" onto a status board without recomputing it and without any test case that could fail.

records.does_not_prove: Recomputing one verdict shows that this verdict follows from its evidence, and says nothing about verdicts nobody recomputed.

reader_ladder.plain: Trust a result only after working it out again from the underlying evidence, and keep a deliberately wrong test case that the check has to reject.

analogy.text: A teacher marks an exam by working each answer out from scratch instead of copying the answer key, and slips in a paper with a planted wrong answer to confirm the marking catches it.

reader_ladder.potential_misread: That checking a result once makes it safe for good, when the check only covers that result against that test.

records.one_line: A claim may be no stronger than what its named checker actually decides, so a checker that confirms one local fact cannot support a sentence about the whole system.
records.deep: P-2 combines AX-1, which limits a claim to the strength of the check that accepted it, with AX-5, which makes a combined result as weak as its weakest part. A verdict that really was recomputed still overclaims if the sentence around it says more than the checker decided. A common case is a validator that confirms a record has the right fields, read as evidence that the property the record names is true. The support checker computes each claim's limit from the specific obligations underneath it, and nobody sets that limit by hand.

formal.reads: A claim's strength is bounded above by the meet of the strengths of exactly the checks that actually decide it; the ceiling is the weakest deciding component, not the most impressive one.

records.governs: How strong a claim may be, given the check that accepted it.
records.requires: Limiting each claim to what its named checker, validator, registry or witness route actually computes, with the limit computed from the underlying obligations.
records.refuses: Using a checker that decides one local contract to support wording about the whole system.

counterexample.text: A component checks that a result record has the expected fields, and a summary page treats that field check as evidence that the underlying property holds everywhere.

records.does_not_prove: Capping a claim at what its checker computes does nothing to make a weak checker stronger.

reader_ladder.plain: A statement can only be as strong as the exact thing the check settled. If a check confirms one small, local fact, the writing around it must stay at that size.

analogy.text: A blood test for iron tells you about iron levels. It gives you no grounds to write 'in perfect health' on the chart.

reader_ladder.potential_misread: That because the underlying check was real, any confident sentence built on it is also safe, when the sentence can only claim what the check decided.

records.one_line: Put trust in a small checker that rereads the producer's certificate and decides, and keep the large producer out of that decision.
records.deep: P-3 applies AX-2. The program you trust should be small enough to read and rerun, while the program that did the work can be as large and opaque as it needs to be. A large model, search or pipeline writes out a certificate, and a small verifier, parser, test harness or registry contract rereads it and gives the verdict. A smaller checker means less code you have to believe in order to believe the verdict. If the producer also gives the verdict, nothing independent has checked it.

counterexample.text: A large model is trusted because it sounds sure of its answer, and no separate checker rereads anything, so the producer is also the judge.

records.does_not_prove: A small checker is easier to audit, and it can still be wrong.

reader_ladder.plain: Put your trust in one small, simple step that redoes the work and decides. The large, complicated program that produced the answer stays out of that decision, because the thing being judged should not judge itself.

reader_ladder.potential_misread: That a capable, confident producer can vouch for its own output, when once the producer decides, no independent check is left.

records.one_line: Permission to change something is worked out from proof references, policy and the current state; a credential, role name or 'trusted session' wording authorizes nothing by itself.
records.deep: P-4 does for permission what P-1 does for evidence. Before an effect happens, the system works out whether it is authorized, using the proof references it can look up, the governing policy, rollback or result records, and the current state of the world. A standing credential, an admin role name or a claim of a trusted session is only identity. This is the confused-deputy problem written as a rule: a component that holds a powerful tool still needs permission for each effect, limited by the declared identity, scope, approval and side-effect records.

formal.reads: Authorization for a subject and an effect is the output of the derivation over the dereferenced tokens, governing policy, proof references, and world state; ambient identity whose tokens dereference to nothing grants nothing. The credential is an input to the derivation, never a substitute for it.

records.refuses: Treating a standing credential, role name, admin wording, trusted session or an available tool as permission on its own.

counterexample.text: A change goes ahead because the caller holds a valid admin credential, and nothing checks that credential against the specific effect, the policy or the current state.

records.does_not_prove: These components show how permission is worked out for the effects they handle, and say nothing about effects that never pass through them.

reader_ladder.plain: Holding a credential, having a role name or being in a 'trusted' session gives no permission to change anything by itself. Permission is worked out again for each action, from the rules and the current situation.

analogy.text: Knowing someone's card number does not move money. For each payment the bank checks this card, this amount and the current account before it lets the transfer through.

reader_ladder.why_it_matters: A component holding broad power cannot be talked into using it for someone else, because each action needs its own permission.
reader_ladder.potential_misread: That a valid credential is enough to act, when the credential is one input and the change still has to be cleared for that exact action against the current state.

records.one_line: A saved result may be reused only if it records a hash of the exact content it was computed from; if that content has changed it must be recomputed, and a matching name allows nothing.
records.deep: P-5 applies AX-4 to reusing earlier work. A saved result, a shared command run, an imported copy of source or a resumed landing attempt may be reused only if it records a hash of the exact content it came from. If the source bytes, the edited files in scope, the parent commit or the fixture input differ, the result is recomputed or the reuse is refused. A name, path or label is a cheap stand-in for that content, and a cache keyed on names serves a stale answer as soon as the content changes.

records.refuses: Serving a cached result looked up by name, path or label after the content behind it has changed.

example.text: The source-import protocol brings public material in with a manifest and a hash for each file, so when the source bytes change the imported copy is recomputed instead of being reused under the same name.

counterexample.text: A resumed landing attempt reuses an earlier result because the task name matches, although the parent commit and the files in scope have changed.

analogy.text: A warranty covers the exact unit whose serial number is on the claim. If a part with a different serial number was swapped in, the matching model name on the box does not carry the warranty over.

A later step may lower a status at any time, and raising one needs a fresh piece of evidence. A summary page can explain why something passed, and it cannot turn a blocked source into a pass.

A report with no findings can mean only that nothing was examined, so a claim of completeness has to cite the places it covered and the evidence for each.

If a function's precondition does not hold, or the library or corpus it needs is missing, it returns a refusal naming the reason and citing the evidence. Returning a forecast past the sample size, a confidence figure with no distribution behind it, or a ready flag while a dependency is missing would be a claim that nothing checked.

The dangerous moment is between two steps, such as a lock released before the lasting record is written or two writers working from a stale parent.

The second is its origin class and usage limit, which say where it may go and how strongly it may be claimed. With only the first, a value can be cached and recomputed correctly with no rule on where it may be shown. With only the second, its trust level is labelled with no way to notice when the source changes.

records.one_line: A write is authorized only as a set of conditions tied to this one transaction: worked-out permission, a declared scope, the parent state it expected, a way to undo it or a declared point of no return, and a record that it landed.
records.deep: P-16 combines AX-3 and AX-9 into one rule about legitimate changes. Permission to change something comes from conditions attached to one transaction, never from holding a credential or being able to reach a tool. Those conditions are permission worked out from policy, proof and current state, a declared write scope the change must stay inside, the parent state the write expected, a way to undo it or a declared irreversible point, and a record that the change landed. The easy failure is the opposite of all five, acting because you can reach the file, on whatever state is there now, with no scope and no undo.

records.requires: Tying the write to this transaction through worked-out permission, a declared scope, the expected parent state, a way to undo it or a declared point of no return, and a landing record.
records.refuses: Treating reach or a standing credential as permission, or writing on whatever state exists without an expected parent, a scope or a way to undo.
records.does_not_prove: One write meeting all five conditions says nothing about other write paths in the system.

The rule combines three obligations: the row's content hash is recorded and rechecked, the change checks the parent state it expected under one writer, and the resulting edge must pass the grammar with result records.

reader_ladder.plain: A new rule does not start to count just because a draft has appeared. Its owner, exact source entry, matching generated copy, passing check and recorded status change all have to land together in one step, and until then it is pending.

analogy.text: A new bylaw takes effect only when it is voted in, signed, entered in the register and marked as in force at one sitting. A draft circulating in the room is still a proposal.

reader_ladder.potential_misread: That once a draft looks complete it is in force, when it counts only after ownership, source, generated copy, check and status change land together.

records.one_line: A missing relation is recorded as a typed gap, and it becomes an edge only when a current source row names it and the target exists.
records.deep: P-19 keeps the system's map accurate as it grows. A missing neighbour is a recorded gap with a type, and before anyone adds it they classify its declared area, source row, target, whether it can be filled, the evidence it needs and its stated limits. A candidate route, a matching file name, a single guess or an out-of-date generated row stays a gap until a current source row names the relation and the builder finds the target. The same rule applies in both directions: doctrine links to the system only through edges taken from source, and the system changes a doctrine rule only through source-owned obligations, witnesses, negative test cases and coverage rows.

formal.reads: An edge is admitted only when a current source row names it and its target resolves under the builder; naming alone does not force admission, and anything short of that is not absence but typed residual pressure in R, carrying its declared domain, evidence floor, and anti-claim until a source row resolves it.

records.refuses: Turning a guess, a matching file name or a generated hint into an edge, in either direction between doctrine and the system.

counterexample.text: A builder adds an edge because two ids share a file name, turning a naming coincidence into a claimed relationship.

records.does_not_prove: Classifying a gap keeps it from being faked, and the gap stays open until a source row names the relation.

reader_ladder.plain: A missing link in the map is a recorded gap with a type, left open until filled properly. You draw the link only once a current source names it and the target really exists.

analogy.text: A transit map draws a line between two stations only when a real service runs between them, however close together they sit.

reader_ladder.why_it_matters: The map stays accurate as it grows, with no invented connections added to make a diagram look complete.
reader_ladder.potential_misread: That a plausible-looking connection is real, when closeness or a shared name is only a reason to check.

records.one_line: A record saved as JSON, markdown or public copy gains authority only once its validator results, evidence references, omissions, stated limits and scope are attached to it.
records.deep: P-20 stops a doctrine record from being trusted just because it exists on disk. Its presence as JSON, a markdown page, a routing edge or a line of public copy says nothing about whether it is current authority. It becomes authority once its validator results, evidence references, declared omissions, stated limits and scope limit are attached and rechecked. This is AX-1 applied to the system's own doctrine, and AX-12 removes any exemption, so a doctrine record passes the same check as any other claim.

formal.reads: A doctrine record may be read as current authority only when it carries its bound result records, evidence refs, declared omissions, anti-claims, and scope limit; missing any of these, it stays a projection below its source.

symbols.meaning: reading the record back as current substrate authority
a doctrine record: its JSON, markdown, routing edge, or public copy
the validator result records are bound on the record (AX-11)

records.refuses: Treating a record's JSON, markdown, routing edge or public copy as authoritative because it exists.

example.text: The release wording gate applies the same claim-language rules to the system's own doctrine copy as to any other component, so a record's public line cannot claim more than its attached checks support.

counterexample.text: A generated doctrine card is cited as current authority for a rule because the JSON exists and the heading sounds confident, with no validator results, omissions or scope limit attached.

records.does_not_prove: Attaching results to a record limits what it may claim and does not make the record correct.

reader_ladder.plain: A record does not become the trusted version just because a readable copy exists. The results of its checks, references to its evidence, what it leaves out and how far it may claim all have to be attached first.

analogy.text: A medicine is cleared for sale once the test results, the list of what was tested, the known side effects and the approved use are all on file. A printed leaflet alone does not clear it.

reader_ladder.potential_misread: That a clear, complete-looking record is authoritative, when authority comes only from the checks and limits attached to it.

records.one_line: Repeating a fixture's verdict, a registry label or a model's answer as true without recomputing it from the evidence underneath.
records.deep: AX-1 forbids accepting a verdict because someone wrote it down. Repeating a label costs nothing and is usually right, so a pipeline that only repeats labels passes its own tests while checking nothing. Recompute the verdict from the underlying evidence and keep a test case with a deliberately wrong label that must fail. If the verdict cannot be recomputed, report a weaker claim.

records.refuses: Repeating a fixture verdict, registry label, Markdown claim or model answer as if repetition made it true.

reader_ladder.potential_misread: That a label being present means someone checked it.

records.one_line: Trusting a claim or an action because of who produced it, what credential they hold or that it worked last time, in place of a checker, a policy or a permission worked out for this request.
records.deep: This is the mistake AX-2 and AX-3 rule out: granting trust because of the sender's identity or badge. Identity is easy to read and is usually correlated with being right, so a system that trusts a known producer, a route that passed before or a long-lived credential works until that producer is wrong or compromised. Producing and checking have to stay separate. A small checker decides the claim from its certificate, and permission for an action is worked out from the tokens, policy and proof references that apply now, never from standing identity or a previous successful run.

records.refuses: Trusting a producer, persona, route, credential or past success in place of a checker, proof, policy or a permission looked up for this request.

counterexample.text: A change to files is allowed because the caller holds a long-lived credential and the same route passed last time, and nothing looks up whether the caller is allowed to make this change now.

records.does_not_prove: Refusing identity-based trust in these replays leaves open whether the permissions that are granted are correct.

reader_ladder.plain: The mistake of letting something through because of who sent it, what badge it carries or that it worked last time, without checking that this request is allowed right now.

analogy.text: A security guard waves someone into a secure room because he recognises their face and they hold an old pass, without looking them up in the access system to see whether they are cleared for that room today.

reader_ladder.potential_misread: That a trusted name, or a pass that worked before, is a safe substitute for checking this request.

records.one_line: Reading a count, a list of names, a passing validator or an evidence-class name as a measure of product maturity, release readiness or correctness of the whole system.
records.deep: A count of passing checks, a list of registered components or a strong evidence label summarises many separate scores, and a high reading on one score can hide a part whose source, freshness or coverage nobody checked. The status of the whole is that of its weakest part, and a part with no supporting evidence counts as blocked, so an average or a raw tally turns a missing check into an apparent pass. Extra passing cases raise the standing of the whole only when they cover a required obligation that had no coverage, raise a score that was below the maximum, or add a missing negative case. Repeating cases over the same inputs changes nothing, and a ranking is only a display of the scores underneath.

formal.reads: Reporting a tally of passing parts as the standing of the whole while some part has no admissible witness, so the claimed status rises above the meet of the parts that an uncovered part should pin to the bottom.

records.refuses: Treating counts, names, passing validators or evidence-class names as product maturity, release readiness or correctness of the whole system.

counterexample.text: A progress page reports that ninety checks pass and calls the system ready for release, while several required parts have no supporting evidence and the gaps are averaged away.

records.does_not_prove: Refusing to read counts and passing validators as a maturity score adds no support to any part.

reader_ladder.plain: The mistake of reading one summary number, such as how many checks passed, as if it said the whole thing is finished or ready, when parts nobody measured could still be failing.

reader_ladder.potential_misread: That more passing checks always means more readiness, when repeating a check that already passed adds nothing.

records.one_line: Reusing a saved result looked up by name, path, route, label or producer after the content it was computed from has changed.
records.deep: This is the mistake AX-4 and AX-10 rule out: treating a name that stays the same as if the content behind it also stayed the same. When the source changes, the name, path or route does not, so the lookup keeps returning yesterday's answer and the pipeline looks fast and consistent while serving a stale value. A saved result is a claim about the inputs it was computed from, and once those inputs change it has no support. Key the cache on a hash of the inputs, reuse a result only when the hash matches, and recompute or refuse when it does not.

records.refuses: Serving a saved result by name, path, route, label or producer after the inputs it was computed from have changed.

records.one_line: Reporting that something is absent because no evidence for it was found, outside a declared finite set of cases that were all checked.

Rounding the gap down to 'nothing there' is the comfortable direction, so a coverage map that marks unexamined areas as clear looks finished when the search simply stopped. The system keeps three states apart: unknown, a claim with no supporting evidence, and a blocked obligation inside a declared domain; merging any of them into 'shown absent' turns an open question into a claim nothing supports.

The figure is right when it is typed, so the extra fields feel like clutter. Later the value changes and the text does not, and a stale figure reads exactly like a current one. P-11 gives the acceptable forms, which are to carry those fields, to keep the value out of permanent text, or to label it as a dated snapshot.

records.one_line: Treating a written rule as binding when the grammar checker has not accepted it and it declares neither the records it must produce nor the limits of its scope.
records.deep: AX-11 forbids letting a sentence govern because it sounds authoritative. A standard, a policy line or a doctrine page binds behaviour only when an executable grammar accepts it and it declares the records it must produce and the limits of its scope; until then it is text for people to read. Writing a confident paragraph is cheap and reads like a rule, so a project can accumulate paragraphs that nothing checks and mistake them for an enforced contract. Run the text through the grammar and attach those obligations and limits, and to give it the weight of a readable summary until that is done.

formal.reads: If an artifact is granted governing authority while it is not accepted by the doctrine grammar, or carries no result-record obligations, or carries no scope limit, reject the authority and treat the prose as a projection.

records.one_line: Excusing the system's own pages, validators, result records or generated summaries from the evidence rules it applies to everything else.
records.deep: This is the exception AX-12 rules out: giving a claim easier treatment because the system is making it about itself. The rules are demanding and the system's own tooling feels trusted, so a generated page, a validator's own verdict, a result record or a coverage summary can end up saying "verified and complete" without meeting the standard applied to outside work. The support evaluator has to meet the support standard it computes, and this page sits below the source it describes and cannot add to that source's authority. Every claim the system makes about itself goes through the same check, so a statement of its own limits does not become a new unchecked claim.

records.one_line: Resting a real claim on a synthetic fixture when real, public-safe material was available, so a made-up input lends the claim strength real inputs never gave it.
records.deep: AX-1, AX-4 and AX-8 together rule this out. A synthetic stand-in was not computed from anything real, so AX-1's checker has nothing to recompute; it is not the hash of any real input, so AX-4 cannot detect when it drifts from what it stands for; and it has no real origin, so its AX-8 provenance label is invented. Synthetic fixtures are convenient and look the same as real ones on the page. The system does use them for testing record shapes and for negative cases, and the rule applies only when real public-safe material exists, in which case a synthetic substitute must not take on the strength of the real input.

records.one_line: Treating a generated result record as if someone wrote it by hand as source, which cuts it off from the inputs it was built from.
records.deep: AX-4 and AX-11 rule out this confusion. A generated record is computed from its inputs, so its identity is the hash of those inputs and its authority is never greater than theirs. Once it is read as source, changes to the inputs no longer force it to be rebuilt, and a hand edit to it has nothing underneath. A generated record often looks hand-written, carries a confident verdict and is already on disk, so citing or editing it is easier than fixing the source and regenerating. The fix keeps the two kinds separate: source is written by hand, generated records are rebuilt from it, and a parity check fails whenever a record no longer matches the source it was built from.

records.one_line: Letting public documentation imply a hosted service, access to an outside service, changes to source files, financial or trading decisions, production readiness, an affiliation or endorsement, or equivalence with the private system, when nothing public backs it.
records.deep: This is a public page claiming powers it cannot back. Any of the seven (a hosted service, access to an outside service, permission to change source files, financial or trading decisions, production readiness, an affiliation or endorsement, or equivalence with the whole private system) can be implied in prose at no cost while nothing behind the page supports it. A power that is supported may be stated within its limits. Three axioms apply. Under AX-5 an unsupported claim within scope counts as blocked, under AX-8 such an implication may reach a public page only through a declared transform, and under AX-12 the system's own text meets the same evidence rules as any other. State only what is supported, and to weaken or withdraw the public claim when the support is missing.
